power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found no imprecise *p* values or *p*-values of exactly zero out of 8 detected.

table.formatted: Among patients with incident, undiagnosed CKD (n=21,995 in Geisinger; n=208,402 in OLDW), CKD diagnosis within 1 year of index date increased from 28.4% in 2008-2012 to 65.7% in 2013-2023 at Geisinger whereas CKD diagnosis decreased from 22.6% to 20.7% at OLDW (DiD estimate 39.1%; 95% CI: 38.1%, 40.1%; p<0.001).
table.expanded: Among patients with incident, undiagnosed CKD (n=21,995 in Geisinger; n=208,402 in OLDW), CKD diagnosis within 1 year of index date increased from 28.4% in 2008-2012 to 65.7% in 2013-2023 at Geisinger whereas CKD diagnosis decreased from 22.6% to 20.7% at OLDW (DiD estimate 39.1%; 95% CI: 38.1%, 40.1%; p<0.001).

table.formatted: Two-sided p<0.05 was considered statistically significant.
table.expanded: Two-sided p<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

table.formatted: The proportion of individuals with a CKD diagnosis code documented during an outpatient encounter within 1 year of the index date at Geisinger increased from 28.4% in 2008-2012 to 65.7% in 2013-2023 (p<0.001).
table.expanded: The proportion of individuals with a CKD diagnosis code documented during an outpatient encounter within 1 year of the index date at Geisinger increased from 28.4% in 2008-2012 to 65.7% in 2013-2023 (p<0.001).

table.formatted: Each 10 percentage-point increase in CKD auto-load was associated with 7.2 percentage-point (95% CI: 6.1%, 8.3%; p<0.001) higher absolute prevalence of CKD diagnosis documentation.
table.expanded: Each 10 percentage-point increase in CKD auto-load was associated with 7.2 percentage-point (95% CI: 6.1%, 8.3%; p<0.001) higher absolute prevalence of CKD diagnosis documentation.

table.formatted: In DiD analysis, the CKD auto-load implementation period was associated with a 39.1% (95% CI: 38.1%, 40.1%; p<0.001) absolute increase in CKD diagnosis at Geisinger compared with the 4 OLDW health systems (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).
table.expanded: In DiD analysis, the CKD auto-load implementation period was associated with a 39.1% (95% CI: 38.1%, 40.1%; p<0.001) absolute increase in CKD diagnosis at Geisinger compared with the 4 OLDW health systems (Figure 3).

table.formatted: The CKD auto-load was associated with OR 1.44 (95% CI 1.32 -1.58; p<0.001) for ACEi/ARB use, OR 1.44 (95% CI: 1.31-1.58; p<0.0001) for statins for those >50 years, and OR 1.30 (95% CI 1.00-1.69; p=0.05) for SGLT2 inhibitors (Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>, Tables <ref type="table">S4-S6</ref>).
